   "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nCOST ALERT: this item follows crude oil and jet fuel prices, read from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) Short-Term Energy Outlook released May 12, 2026, the EIA daily prices page, the St. Louis Fed jet fuel series and the IATA Jet Fuel Price Monitor. Signal event: «The Brent crude oil spot price increased sharply in April , reaching a high of $138 per barrel (b) on April 7 and averaging $117/b for the month, as the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz tightened global oil supplies.» The same outlook expects Brent «keeping Brent prices around $106/b in May and June». The EIA daily page then shows Brent below that path: «Wholesale Spot Petroleum Prices, 6/04/26 Close Product Area Price Percent Change* Crude Oil ($/barrel) WTI 96.83 -2.9 Brent 98.98 -2.7». Against the April high of $138 per barrel that is a fall, and against the outlook's May and June level of $106/b it is lower still, so by early June the spot price sat under the path the May outlook had drawn.\n\nJet fuel, the product an air quote follows, moved the other way at the start of June. The St. Louis Fed series for kerosene-type jet fuel on the US Gulf Coast reads «Observations 2026-06-01: 3.569 | Dollars per Gallon, Not Seasonally Adjusted | Daily» against «2026-05-29:  3.237», a rise from the last day of May to the first of June. The IATA monitor, a separate global series, says «The global average jet fuel price last week fell 11.4% compared to the week before to $141.64/bbl.» The monitor defines its series as refinery prices: «The Jet Fuel Price Index and price data show the average prices paid at the refinery for aviation jet fuel for the reported week.» The pages hold no value for these series after early June, so the movement since then is not stated here.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the sources name the supply side of the oil market, not a buyer or a seller of freight. The EIA states: «We assess that Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, and Bahrain collectively shut in 10.5 million barrels per day (b/d) of crude oil production in April.» It adds: «The UAE announced its departure from OPEC, effective May 1, 2026.» The consequence the EIA draws is about spare capacity: «Because the UAE held spare crude oil production capacity, we now expect OPEC’s spare capacity to average 2.5 million b/d in 2027, compared with our previous forecast of 3.8 million b/d.» *Analytical inference:* these are the parties whose output decisions the EIA ties to the Brent path, because the outlook links the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to the price move and the return of Middle East production to the fall it expects. The pages state no interest, bid or intent of any one producer, so none is attributed. The jet fuel series are published by the EIA via the St. Louis Fed and by IATA with data licensed from S&P Global Energy; neither page describes a party seeking a price outcome.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the EIA outlook names the event that moves this signal, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the return of Middle East oil production. Its stated assumption: «This report assumes that the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed until late May, with shipping traffic beginning to pick up in June.» Its stated consequence for price: «As oil production in the Middle East rises, we expect crude oil prices to fall, dropping to an average of $89/b in 4Q26 and $79/b in 2027.»\n\n- May 12, 2026: the EIA outlook this brief reads was released («Release Date: May 12, 2026»). The release is past, and the pages hold no later outlook.\n- June 9, 2026: the same page named «Next Release Date: June 9, 2026». That date is also past and no outlook of that release is held, so the path below is the May view, not the current one.\n- 2027: the outlook expects a Brent average of $79/b for the year.\n\n*Analytical inference:* 4Q26 is the quarter now running, and the pages hold no observed Brent or jet fuel price for it, so the $89/b average cannot be checked against anything held here. A quote priced off the May path rests on an assumption the pages themselves tie to the Strait reopening on the dates above.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe pages state no rule for how a jet fuel price enters an air freight rate and no marine fuel price, so the pass-through below is labelled analysis. *Operational implication:* a carrier rate or surcharge that follows a published jet fuel series moves with it after a lag the pages do not give; a quote held across a long validity period is exposed upward if jet fuel stays near its early June reading of 3.569 dollars a gallon and downward if the outlook's fall to $89/b arrives. The size of that effect for any one air lane needs the carrier's own surcharge terms, which the pages do not hold.\n\nFor road, the EIA daily page gives the retail diesel level against which a road fuel cost can be read: «Retail Petroleum Prices ( AAA ), 6/04/26 ($/gallon) Regular Gasoline U.S. Average 4.22 -0.5 Diesel U.S. Average 5.38 -0.3». The CME page states a limit on how far crude carries through: «Crude oil costs account for 56% of the average price of a gallon of heating oil or ultra-low-sulfur diesel.» That share is given for heating oil and ultra-low-sulfur diesel, not for jet fuel, so it does not size the jet fuel effect. *Analytical inference:* because crude is only part of the diesel price per that statement, a Brent fall does not cut a road fuel charge one for one.\n\nCorridor identity: the pages name no origin-destination port pair and no transport mode together; they are global and US Gulf Coast price series. The pages give no biofuel or marine fuel price, so the premium of those fuels over the fossil reference is not stated.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor and no operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Name the public sources of the fuel figure: the EIA outlook, the EIA daily prices page, the St. Louis Fed jet fuel series and the IATA monitor.\n- Say that the Brent peak of $138 per barrel on April 7 was a spot high, and that the May outlook expected «keeping Brent prices around $106/b in May and June», so a quote built on the peak overstates the later path the outlook drew.\n- Ask the client whether its air rate indexes fuel to a published series, and to which one, before the next rate review.\n- Do not present the early June readings as the current price: the pages hold nothing after them.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: COST ALERT: A pricing lead, on the next air quote run, writes the jet fuel series each quote follows (the St. Louis Fed Gulf Coast kerosene-type series or the IATA monitor) beside the quote date and the quote validity length.\n\n- A contract lead adds, at the next air rate renewal, a clause naming the jet fuel series and the day of the week the surcharge resets from it.\n- A carrier-relations lead asks each air carrier in writing which published jet fuel series its fuel surcharge follows and how many weeks it lags that series.\n- A data lead pulls the EIA outlook released after May 12, 2026 and sets the Brent and jet fuel path in the quote file so the May path is replaced.\n\n## 8. Sources\n\n- US Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook (statistical agency forecast), https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/\n- US Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy Daily Prices (statistical agency data), https://eia.gov/todayinenergy/prices.php\n- St. Louis Fed FRED, Kerosene-Type Jet Fuel Prices: US Gulf Coast, series from the US Energy Information Administration (statistical data), https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DJFUELUSGULF\n- International Air Transport Association, Jet Fuel Price Monitor, data licensed from S&P Global Energy (industry association), https://www.iata.org/en/publications/economics/fuel-monitor/\n- CME Group, crude oil futures page (exchange), https://www.cmegroup.com/markets/energy/crude-oil/light-sweet-crude.html",

   "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: this item reads the World Bank Group's transport strategy as it publishes it on its Transport topic page and in its results story on how better transport drives opportunity. Signal event, the size of the money behind it: «With an active transport portfolio of nearly $45 billion as of end-February 2026 – including around $4 billion in own-account commitments by IFC – the World Bank Group is the largest provider of development financing for transport in the world.» The same page adds the year's flow: «In FY25 , the World Bank approved 53 new transport operations for a total of $11.2 billion.»\n\nThe Bank gives the reason for the spending in its own words: «Each year through 2030, Low-and middle-income countries require $417 billion in resilient transport investments.» The pages do not rank the Bank-funded places for freight, so the list in section 4 is only what the pages name.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the World Bank Group and its private-sector arms. The pages name IFC and MIGA as the arms that mobilise financing and guarantees: «The Tanger Med Port Complex has received support from the World Bank Group through its private-sector arms, IFC and MIGA, which have helped mobilize financing and guarantees for port expansion and modernization projects.» A second vehicle is a donor fund: «The Global Facility to Decarbonize Transport (GFDT) is a multi-donor trust fund managed by the World Bank that aims to accelerate innovation and investment in climate-smart mobility solutions in low and middle-income countries.» The pages state no interest of any shipping line, forwarder or carrier in these programmes, so none is attributed.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the Bank states what has to be in place for transport spending to turn into growth: «Creating efficient, resilient, and affordable transportation systems can unleash economic growth and create jobs but requires private sector mobilization in coordination with public spending.» *Analytical inference:* the condition is private sector money alongside public money, so the signal turns into commercial pressure on a lane when private financiers and operators commit to it, not when the Bank approves a loan; the pages name no date for that on any one lane.\n\n- 2030: the Bank says low and middle-income countries need resilient transport investment each year through 2030, the horizon of the need it states.\n- 2042: the Bank projects, for India's freight corridors: «By 2042, total cumulative emissions reductions are projected to reach 13.19 million tons, a reduction of 57 percent from pre-project levels in 2010.»\n\nThe pages put one number on the scale of the gap: «Each year through 2030, Low-and middle-income countries require $417 billion in resilient transport investments.» Neither date is a deadline for a freight operator; both are the Bank's own planning horizons.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe Bank's pages describe results on named corridors, not a rate change on any lane. *Operational implication:* where the Bank funds a rail line or port upgrade, the lane's transit time and handling cost baseline can move, so a quote built on today's baseline for that lane needs a review once the works are in service.\n\n- India, dedicated freight rail: «In India, from 2011 to 2024, 1,200 kilometers (km) of new dedicated freight tracks were built, freight train capacity was boosted fourfold, train operational speeds were increased, logistics costs reduced by up to $58 million, about 9 million days of employment generated, and emissions (in 2024 alone) cut by 55,000 tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO₂e).» «Each kilometer-long freight train on the EDFC replaces about 72 trucks, helping to reduce highway congestion, improve safety, and lower air pollution.» *Analytical inference:* where a freight train replaces trucks, road haulage on that corridor faces rail capacity as an alternative; the pages give no tariff for rail, so the price advantage is not stated.\n- Cameroon, Douala to N'Djamena corridor: «In Cameroon, road and rail infrastructure upgrades along the Douala–N’Djamena corridor lowered container shipping costs by over 7 percent between 2012 and 2022.»\n- Uzbekistan: «In Uzbekistan, from 2015 to 2020, a new mixed-used rail link improved connectivity for over 740,000 people, cut passenger travel costs by 33 percent, reduced trip delays from 95 percent to 10 percent, and reduced freight costs for key goods by up to 80 percent.»\n- Morocco, Tanger Med: «These investments—including support for a €476 million expansion and upgrades to truck and passenger terminals—aim to strengthen Morocco’s role as a global logistics hub and boost trade connectivity between Africa, Europe, and global markets.»\n\nThe effect on container movement can be read from the Bank's own logistics data: «Indicator Container import dwell time 2023-2024 | 163 Economies | Updated Annual», where the measure is defined as «The container import dwell time is calculated as the time between the discharge of a full container from the vessel at the port of arrival (port of entry) until the time the container exits port's premises by truck or rail.» The pages give no figure for a given port and no rule for how a cost change reaches a forwarder's invoice, so the pass-through is not stated.\n\nCorridor identity: the pages name corridors and a port complex but no origin-destination port pair with a transport mode stated together.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor and no operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say that the World Bank Group is financing transport at scale: «In FY25 , the World Bank approved 53 new transport operations for a total of $11.2 billion.»\n- Say that the Bank's results are for named programmes: for example, «Each kilometer-long freight train on the EDFC replaces about 72 trucks, helping to reduce highway congestion, improve safety, and lower air pollution.»\n- Ask the client which of its lanes touch the corridors in section 4 and whether its quotes assume today's transit time on them.\n- Do not present the Bank's estimates as forecasts for any lane: the pages state results and plans for the programmes they name, not a freight rate.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: MONITORING: A trade-lane lead, at the next quarterly lane review, adds a line for each corridor the World Bank pages name (India's dedicated freight tracks, the Douala to N'Djamena road and rail corridor, the Uzbekistan rail link, the Tanger Med port complex) and records beside it the freight cost or time figure the Bank states and the transit time the desk quotes today.\n\n- An operations lead pulls the container import dwell time figures from the Bank's Logistics Performance Index data page for the countries on its lanes and sets them beside its own port-to-gate times.\n- A sales lead keeps one client answer ready on how the Bank's rail and port investment could change transit on a named corridor, using only the results the pages state.\n- A contract lead flags, at the next renewal of any contract on the named corridors, a clause that lets the transit-time basis be reopened once new works are in service.\n\n## 8. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: this item reads Singapore's maritime decarbonisation plan, the Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint, and the activity around it. Signal event: «The Maritime Singapore Decarbonisation Blueprint: Working Towards 2050 charts ambitious and concrete long-term strategies to build a sustainable Maritime Singapore.» The factsheet carrying the targets is marked «Published 09 Mar 2022», and the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) backs it with money: «To move more decisively on maritime decarbonisation, MPA will commit additional funds of at least $300 million to support initiatives outlined in the Blueprint.»\n\nThe Blueprint sets a target for each of seven focus areas. For port terminals: «At least 60% reduction in absolute emissions from 2005 levels by 2030 Net zero emissions by 2050». For domestic harbour craft: «All harbour craft will operate on low-carbon energy solutions by 2030 and full electric propulsion and net zero fuels by 2050». For the Singapore Registry of Ships: «working towards 50% of the SRS fleet to be green ships by 2050». For fuels, the plan is to «Be ready for a multi-fuel bunkering transition to support the future of international shipping, by supplying low and zero-carbon marine fuels including biofuels, methanol, ammonia, and potentially hydrogen». *Analytical inference:* the plan is a Singapore authority's own ambition for its terminals, craft, registry and bunkering, so it signals which fuels Singapore intends to supply and does not by itself bind a carrier or a cargo owner; the pages state no rule that reaches a forwarder's contract.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the Singapore authority and a funded industry body. The Blueprint was «Developed by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) in consultation with industry partners, the Blueprint will contribute to Singapore’s commitments under the United Nations’ 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda, Paris Agreement and the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships». A second body is a centre that works through pilots: «Launched on 1 August 2021, the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation is a non-profit organisation that supports the decarbonisation of the maritime sector through pilots and trials.» It reports its reach: «Since its founding, GCMD has expanded its ecosystem to include more than 130 centre- and project-level partners contributing funds, expertise, and in-kind support to pilot, accelerate the deployment, and scale the adoption of decarbonisation solutions.» On the fuel side MPA also works with an energy body: «MPA and the International Energy Agency (IEA) signed an MoU on the Energy Transition of the Maritime and Port Industries and announced the partnership at the event.» MPA's Chief Executive states the aim: «A key priority is to establish the end-to-end value chains for these new fuels.» The pages do not say that any one fuel will be mandated.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the page that carries the clearest route from plan to cost is the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General's statement at the 2024 conference: «We are on track to adopt mid-term measures by late 2025 to cut GHG emissions, to reach net zero targets. These mid-term measures, which are currently being discussed by Member States, include a goal-based marine fuel standard, and a pricing mechanism for maritime GHG emissions.» The same statement gives the checkpoints those measures serve: «with indicative checkpoints to reach by 2030 (cut GHG emissions by at least 20%, striving for 30%), and 2040 (cut GHG emissions by at least 70%, striving for 80%)» *Analytical inference:* a fuel standard and a price on maritime emissions would change fuel and emissions cost for shipping, and the checkpoints set the 2030 and 2040 pace they are meant to meet; the pages hold no confirmation that the late 2025 adoption happened, and that date is now past.\n\n- 2030: port terminals, harbour craft and the methanol outlook all carry a 2030 date in the Blueprint pages; the targets for the Singapore terminals and craft sit in section 1, and the supply outlook is «On aggregate, these projects have the potential to supply over one MTPA of low-carbon methanol by 2030, subject to commercial decisions and global developments.»\n- 2040: the IMO indicative checkpoint of a cut of at least 70%, striving for 80%, for the entire shipping sector, per the statement above.\n- 2050: the net zero date for Singapore port terminals and for full electric propulsion and net zero fuels in harbour craft, and the date for half of the registry fleet to be green ships.\n- 2025: the release marked «Published 17 Apr 2024» said «The standards for methanol are expected to be published by EnterpriseSG in 2025.» That year is past and the pages hold no publication notice.\n\nOn methanol demand the same release says «the demand for methanol as a marine fuel in Singapore can potentially exceed one million tons per annum (MTPA) before 2030, subject to the pace of developments of supply chains, infrastructure, and regulations globally». Its licence step, «MPA will call for applications for a licence to supply methanol as a marine fuel in Singapore by the end of the year.», was due in 2024 and the pages hold no later notice. Interest in supplying was strong: «There was strong interest in the EOI. MPA received a total of 50 submissions, out of which 40% of them proposed end-to-end solutions covering all three areas highlighted in the EOI.»\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe pages state no surcharge, premium or tariff for any of these fuels, so the cost route below is labelled analysis. *Operational implication:* an ocean carrier that bunkers methanol, ammonia or biofuel in Singapore pays whatever those fuels cost, and a carrier rate or fuel surcharge can follow; the pages give no price and no pass-through rule, so the size and timing depend on each carrier's own terms.\n\nWhat exists at Singapore is shown in the pages. The release marked «Published 17 Apr 2024» reports «Following the completion of the world’s first ship-to-containership methanol bunkering in Singapore last year» (so in the year before that release), and «the world’s first ocean-going ammonia-powered vessel, Fortescue Green Pioneer, successfully conducted its first fuel trial in Singapore». *Analytical inference:* the centre sits in «Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering hub and busiest transshipment port», so what it pilots is tested at the port the pages describe as the largest bunkering hub.\n\nFor a lane between Singapore and Australia the pages add a corridor: «The Singapore-Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor (GDSC) was formalised in March 2024 through a memorandum of understanding.» Its first action area is «Enabling the supply of zero or near-zero greenhouse gas emission maritime fuels between Singapore and Australia». «Australian port authorities currently involved under the GDSC include Fremantle Ports Authority, Pilbara Ports Authority, Ports Victoria and Gladstone Ports Corporation.» One of them has a stated task: «Pilbara Ports Authority–bunkering standards and procedures for zero or near-zero emission maritime fuels». *Analytical inference:* the pages tie the corridor to fuel supply between Singapore and Australia and give each port authority a task; they say nothing about cargo rates on it.\n\nCorridor identity: the pages name Singapore, Australia and four Australian port authorities, but no origin-destination port pair with a transport mode stated together.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor of the Blueprint and no operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say that Singapore's authority has set out a plan for terminals, harbour craft, its ship registry and green fuels, and that it is a plan, not a rule on carriers.\n- Say that the Singapore-Australia corridor is a government arrangement: «The Singapore-Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor (GDSC) was formalised in March 2024 through a memorandum of understanding.»\n- Ask the client whether its ocean contracts carry a fuel surcharge and which fuel it is indexed to, before any green-fuel option is priced.\n- Do not present the IMO measures as in force: the page says they were being discussed and expected, and holds no adoption notice.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: MONITORING: An ocean procurement lead, at the next carrier tender that includes Singapore or Singapore to Australia lanes, adds a question asking each carrier which of the fuels the Blueprint names (biofuels, methanol, ammonia) it bunkers in Singapore and whether it will charge a green-fuel premium or surcharge, and records each answer beside the quote.\n\n- A contract lead adds, at the next ocean contract renewal, a clause that sets how a cost from an IMO fuel standard or a price on maritime emissions is passed on, so the route is agreed before any such measure binds.\n- A lane lead lists which of the four Australian port authorities named in the corridor sit on the desk's Singapore to Australia lanes and notes their bunkering tasks beside each lane.\n- A sales lead keeps a short client answer ready on what the Blueprint is and is not, using only the statements in section 1.\n\n## 8.    "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: this item reads the ASEAN regional transport plan and its successor. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: this item reads the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) Group's transport framework for Latin America and the Caribbean and the money moving under it. Signal event, the newest financing the page shows, dated «The operation will improve transportation, expand access to markets and services for... February 11, 2026»: «The Board of Executive Directors of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) has approved a $200 million loan to finance the construction of a vital section of the Bi-Oceanic Corridor in Paraguay.» The framework behind it: «The Sector Framework Document guides the work carried out by the IDB Group with the countries and governments of Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) in the transportation sector.» Its stated areas of action include «the improvement of logistics for competitiveness and regional integration, the sustainability of the transport system, its digital transformation, and the improvement of its institutional framework».\n\nThe Bank gives the scale of the gap in its own words: «According to IDB calculations, the region needs to double its infrastructure investments over the next 30 years to increase average growth from 2.4% to 5.0%.» It also states a cost link that matters to freight: «The poor quality and limited capacity of transport infrastructure have a negative impact on the prices of products and services.» *Analytical inference:* the framework and the loans are the Bank's financing choices, so they show where corridor, port and road works are being paid for; they set no rule for a carrier or a shipper, and the pages state no rate effect.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the IDB Group, with national governments and the companies named in its project lists. The Bank describes how its projects are built: «The projects we finance are usually implemented through public-private partnerships (PPPs) with private companies bearing the initial costs and sharing the risks, management responsibility, and potential future profits.» A second programme sets the regional frame: «South Connection is a joint commitment by South American countries to develop strategic corridors integrating transport, energy, and digital infrastructure.» «With the support of 11 countries, South Connection aims to transform infrastructure, streamline trade, and attract investment». The IDB Invest page lists projects with the company and the amount, for example «Financing for the Expansion of the Port of Mataran... Terminal Internacional del Sur SA Peru Financing amount $ 125,000,000» and «Paraguay Route 1 Project – Mercosur Routes Consort... Consorcio Rutas del Mercosur Paraguay Financing amount $ 135,000,000». The pages name no forwarder or carrier interest in these projects.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the pages name no completion or opening date for any financed corridor section, so the date at which a loan turns into changed transit conditions on a lane is not stated. What the programme says it will deliver: «We work with countries to improve logistics services, modernize border crossings, and streamline customs operations. Faster and more predictable trade systems are essential to reduce costs, shorten transit times, and improve reliability.» *Analytical inference:* the change reaches a lane when a financed section opens and a border crossing or a customs step is modernised, which the pages describe as an aim and date nowhere.\n\n- Dec 17, 2025: the IDB blog on the regional transport dialogue is dated «Dec 17, 2025»; its forward statement is «demand for passenger and freight transport is expected to nearly double by 2050».\n- October 2023: the pages give «Published: October 2023» for the IDB report Transportation 2050, which is past.\n- 2050: the year to which the IDB expects transport demand to nearly double, a forecast and not a deadline.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe pages state no rate, tariff or transit time for any lane, so the implications below are labelled analysis. *Operational implication:* where the Bank finances a road section, a port expansion or a border crossing, the transit time and handling cost baseline on that lane can move once the works are in service, so a quote built on today's baseline for the lane needs review at that point.\n\nWhat the financed works are, as the pages list them: «South Connection supports sustainable investments to build and modernize roads, ports, waterways, power grids, and digital networks—particularly along key bi-oceanic corridors that unlock regional and global trade potential.» The Peru port expansion and the Paraguay Route 1 project both appear in the project list quoted in section 2.\n\nOn the emissions side, the Bank's 2023 report states: «Road transportation accounts for 92% of total emissions, domestic aviation for 4%, domestic navigation for 2%, and rail transportation for 1%.» The report states no measure and does not say how much of the road share is freight.\n\nCorridor identity: the pages name the Bi-Oceanic Corridor in Paraguay and the corridors of South Connection, but no origin-destination port pair with a transport mode stated together.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor and no operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say that the IDB Group has approved a $200 million loan for a section of the Bi-Oceanic Corridor in Paraguay, and that the Bank frames its transport work as a system of services, institutions and technology as well as infrastructure.\n- Say that South Connection is a joint South American programme: «South Connection is a joint commitment by South American countries to develop strategic corridors integrating transport, energy, and digital infrastructure.»\n- Ask the client which South American lanes cross a border or use a port named in the IDB lists, so the works can be read against those lanes.\n- Do not present the loans as finished works: the pages state approvals and aims, not opening dates.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: MONITORING: A South America lane lead, at the next quarterly lane review, lists the corridor sections and ports the IDB pages name (the Bi-Oceanic Corridor section in Paraguay, the Paraguay Route 1 project, the Peru port expansion) and records beside each the border-crossing time and transit-time assumption used in current quotes.\n\n- A customs lead notes the South Connection aim to modernise border crossings and streamline customs operations, and lists the border crossings on the desk's South American lanes so any change can be compared with today's clearance times.\n- A contract lead adds, at the next renewal of a contract on those lanes, a clause that lets the transit-time basis be reopened when a financed section opens.\n- A sales lead keeps one client answer ready on what the IDB framework is and is not, using only the statements in section 1.\n\n## 8.    "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: this item follows the United States federal electric vehicle charging programme run by the Joint Office of Energy and Transportation (the Joint Office, a body of the Department of Energy and the Department of Transportation) and the funding behind it. Signal event, from an Eno Center for Transportation article dated «January 30, 2026»: a federal court issued a final judgment on the funding freeze, which the article reports as determining «USDOT’s February to August pause of the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program to be a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act.»\n\nThe programme is far from built out. The same article reports that the programme made available «$4.4 billion», that «$94 million has been spent by» states, and that states have obligated «$1.4 billion» «in funds for future charging stations» through «2028». The US Government Accountability Office (GAO) counted earlier: «As of April 2025, 384 NEVI- and CFI-funded chargers were open to the public.» The article continues: «According to September 2025 data», «there are 80 NEVI-funded charging locations with over 370» individual fast chargers opened through the programme. *Analytical inference:* the money is allocated but mostly unspent, so charging capacity along US highways is arriving slowly; the pages tie the slowness to the 2025 pause and to reimbursement timing, and no page states a date by which the network is complete.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the Joint Office, the Federal Highway Administration and the states. The GAO states how the Joint Office came about: «DOE and DOT documented in 2021 how they would align their resources and expertise in establishing the Joint Office to facilitate an interagency approach to supporting charging infrastructure.» Industry is invited in: «Private sector companies are invited to bid into the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program and Charging and Fueling Infrastructure Program opportunities released by states and communities.» On the standards side, the Joint Office and the SAE Industry Technologies Consortia (SAE ITC) «announced a common EVPKI framework that will enable secure automatic authentication as soon as drivers plug in» (dated «Dec. 4, 2024»). For freight, the Joint Office's strategy: «National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy sets an actionable vision and comprehensive approach to accelerating the deployment of a world-class freight network in the United States.» «It is an all-of-government approach to align, unlock, and unleash medium- and heavy-duty vehicle infrastructure and bolster electric grid and hydrogen planning.» *Analytical inference:* the strategy sets a federal vision for medium- and heavy-duty vehicle infrastructure, and the pages tie the funded stations to state plans; they state no commitment by any freight operator or carrier.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: what turns this from a programme into a charging network a truck operator can plan on is money reaching the ground and the funding rules holding. Two facts bear on it. The funding rules were frozen once: «In February 2025, Secretary Duffy’s Department of Transportation froze the NEVI program for review», and the plaintiff states said that money «was available for the States to obligate for NEVI projects; after February 6, that number dropped to zero.» The programme's money may also move: «states must now consider the potential impact of the pending FY 2026 appropriations bill, which transfers $879 million in NEVI funds into other Federal Highway Administration programs.» *Analytical inference:* the article dated January 30, 2026 calls the appropriations bill pending, and the pages hold no later outcome, so whether the $879 million moved is not known here.\n\n- Dec. 4, 2024: the Joint Office and SAE ITC announce the common authentication framework; the release says «New framework will enable industry-wide seamless, secure electric vehicle charging experience across all public stations with testing starting in 2025», and the pages hold no test result.\n- February 2025: the Department of Transportation freezes the programme for review; the court later finds the pause unlawful.\n- January 30, 2026: the Eno article reports the final judgment and the funding position.\n- 2028: states have obligated «$1.4 billion» for future charging stations through «2028».\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe pages give no charging price, no truck charging site and no freight rate, so the implications below are labelled analysis. *Operational implication:* a quote for a US highway lane that assumes public charging on the route depends on that charging being open; the pages show that the federally funded network is small and slow to open, so a lane quote that depends on it needs a fallback.\n\nWhat is built: the GAO counted «As of April 2025, 384 NEVI- and CFI-funded chargers were open to the public.» By September 2025 the Eno article cites «there are 80 NEVI-funded charging locations with over 370» individual fast chargers. Against that, it cites private data that «the US has a total of 12,375 charging stations with 64,486» ports, so the federally funded programme is a small part of US public charging. The programme's design target is «the program aimed to help build the national electric vehicle charging infrastructure, with the goal of having an EV station every 50 miles on highways.», and the Eno article states a technical floor: «Charging stations under NEVI must have a minimum power of 150 kilowatts». *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the 150 kilowatt minimum, which the Eno article attributes to NEVI, is the standard in force for the stations of a given state, which the federal rule text for the programme and the state plan would settle. The GAO adds a limit on how far results can be judged: «The Joint Office has taken some steps to assess its activities, but GAO found it generally has not defined performance goals with measurable targets and time frames for its activities.» The pages do not say whether any NEVI-funded location can charge a medium- or heavy-duty truck.\n\nCorridor identity: the pages name US highways and a national freight corridor strategy, but no origin-destination port pair with a transport mode stated together.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor and no operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say that the US federal charging programme has been held up by a pause that a court found unlawful, and that most of its money has been committed but not yet spent.\n- Say that the Joint Office has a freight strategy: «National Zero-Emission Freight Corridor Strategy sets an actionable vision and comprehensive approach to accelerating the deployment of a world-class freight network in the United States.»\n- Ask the client which US lanes its electric trucks run and where it charges today, before any public charging is assumed in a quote.\n- Do not present the programme as a finished network: the article counts «there are 80 NEVI-funded charging locations with over 370» individual fast chargers opened through it.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: MONITORING: A US road freight lead, at the next quarterly lane review, lists the US lanes where the desk quotes or plans electric trucks and records for each whether a NEVI-funded charging location is open on the route, using the state's own list, with the depot charging assumption used in the quote.\n\n- A procurement lead asks each charging network used for fleet charging whether it supports Plug and Charge now that the common framework has been announced, and records the answer beside the network.\n- A contract lead adds, at the next US electric haulage contract, a clause that sets what happens to the rate if a planned public charging site on the route does not open.\n- A sales lead keeps one client answer ready on what the Joint Office is and is not, using only the statements in section 1 and section 2.\n\n## 8.    "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nCOST ALERT: air cargo prices stayed far above last year through May, and the sources tie it to the Middle East war. Signal event: «Global air cargo spot rates rose 41% year-on-year in May to an average of $3.40 per kg, driven by resilient demand, constrained capacity and ongoing geopolitical disruptions, according to Xeneta.» The same update, dated «6 June 2026», adds: «The market update, released in June, showed that global air cargo demand increased 4% year-on-year while capacity recovered to 1% above last year's level.» The International Air Transport Association (IATA) release of «Date: 28 May 2026» states for April: «Total demand, measured in cargo tonne-kilometers (CTK), increased by 4.0% compared to April 2025 levels (+4.0% for international operations). Capacity, measured in available cargo tonne-kilometers (ACTK), decreased by -0.4% compared to April 2025 (-0.9% for international operations).» Its cost context: «Jet fuel prices rose sharply in April, up 121.1% year-on-year, alongside a 77.7% increase in crude oil prices.»\n\nA second rate series, WorldACD data for week 21, gives a different level: «average full market air cargo rates were flat in week 21 at $3.23 per kilo, but compared to the same period last year, restricted capacity, high jet fuel costs, and greater use of freighter aircraft drove a rate increase of 35%.» and «Average worldwide spot rates edged up by a further 1% week on week to $3.75 per kilo». *Analytical inference:* the two sources measure different things (the Xeneta figure is a May average, the WorldACD figures are for one week), so they are not to be subtracted from each other; both show rates well above last year. Capacity is the other half: «compared to pre-war levels in week 7, capacity is down by nearly one third (32%), largely due to reductions for the Gulf, where capacity is barely half its pre-war levels (48%)».\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the Gulf carriers and hubs whose capacity is cut, the freighter operators filling the gap, and shippers who buy time. IATA's Director General describes the cause: «Severe disruption at major Gulf hubs due to the war in the Middle East continued to reshape trade routes and constrain capacity on key corridors.» Xeneta's Chief Airfreight Officer describes how shippers respond: shippers are «they are adjusting and buying time by temporarily accepting the surcharges that come with extending existing capacity contracts». The load on particular lanes is concentrated: «Artificial intelligence-related shipments, particularly semiconductors and data centre equipment, continued to drive strong transpacific demand.» On fuel, the WorldACD summary says: «Rising fuel costs have also led airlines to reduce or cancel unprofitable routes, particularly regional services operated by narrowbody aircraft, although the impact on cargo capacity has remained limited.» «Airlines cut 13,000 flights in May, and industry observers expect further schedule changes as aviation fuel prices are unlikely to decline significantly in the near term.» A forwarder, Flexport, is selling a way round: «Flexport has launched Sea-Air Express, our new multimodal solution for shippers looking to circumvent Middle East disruptions.» *Analytical inference:* shippers are choosing between paying surcharges and testing a sea-air option, and the sources say the cut flights have had limited impact on cargo capacity; the vendor's claim «Sea-Air Express can deliver cargo from Asia to Europe in as few as 27 days, at rates up to 41% below pure air freight.» is Flexport's own and is not checked by any other page.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the sources do not name one trigger but a set of easing and tightening signals. For easing: «Despite the sharp increase in rates, Xeneta believes pricing pressures on shippers may begin to ease in June as capacity returns and demand growth moderates.» «Long-term contract rates, which increased 22% year-on-year, eased after reaching a peak at the end of April, suggesting the market may have already passed its pricing high point.» «Further moderation is expected during the northern hemisphere summer period, when additional passenger aircraft capacity typically returns to the market.» Xeneta's closing line: «Don’t expect a hot summer for air freight demand.» For new cost on the e-commerce flow, the same article says «the European Union prepares to remove its €150 de minimis exemption from 1 July, replacing it with a €3 duty per imported item and an additional €2 handling fee expected later in the year». For tariffs it adds: «The proposal remains under review ahead of hearings scheduled for July.» *Analytical inference:* the rate path therefore turns on how fast Gulf capacity returns, which the WorldACD data show is slow (see section 1), and on whether summer passenger capacity arrives as expected; the pages hold nothing after early June, so whether rates eased is not known here.\n\n- 28 May 2026: IATA publishes its April air cargo data.\n- 6 June 2026: Xeneta's May update is reported, expecting pricing pressure to ease in June as capacity returns; that window is past and no confirming figure is held.\n- 1 July: the EU de minimis exemption is to be removed, per the article dated 6 June 2026; the date is past and the pages do not confirm it took effect.\n- July: US Trade Representative hearings on the proposed additional tariffs, also past, with no outcome held.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe sources give one sourced pass-through: shippers are paying surcharges to extend capacity contracts (section 2). They give no jet fuel surcharge rule and no rate per lane for forwarder invoices, so the lines below are labelled analysis. *Operational implication:* an air quote built on a rate from May rests on a price the sources expect to ease, so a long validity period carries risk in both directions: too high if rates fall as expected, too low if the Gulf disruption deepens. The contract-versus-spot gap is stated: contract rates rose 22% year-on-year against 41% for spot (section 3). *Analytical inference:* on those two figures, buying on contract has moved less than buying spot; the sources do not say what any one forwarder pays.\n\nThe lane picture differs by corridor. IATA's table for April: «Europe-Asia +16.2% 38 consecutive months of growth 21.5% Europe-Middle East -25.9% 2 months of contraction 5.2% Europe-North America -1.0% 2 months of contraction 13.5% Middle East-Asia -22.4% 2 months of contraction 7.4%», the last figure on each lane being its share of industry traffic. Gulf-linked lanes are in contraction and Europe-Asia is growing. In the Xeneta report, missile activity slowed capacity recovery into the Middle East, «keeping rates on routes from Europe, South Asia and Southeast Asia to the region significantly above pre-conflict levels. Some spot rates were up by as much as 113% compared with late February.» *Analytical inference:* a quote to the Middle East from Europe, South Asia or Southeast Asia carries the largest rate risk of the lanes named, and the Europe-Asia lane the strongest demand; the pages name no per-lane rate for either.\n\nOn e-commerce, Xeneta reports «China's low-value and e-commerce exports, which fell 11% year-on-year in April, marking a fifth consecutive monthly decline», and that «Shipments to the United States dropped 33%». Because the sources say the apparent declines may reflect a shift to consolidated bulk air freight, the volume signal for forwarders is uncertain.\n\nCorridor identity: the pages name lanes by region pair, such as Europe-Asia and Europe-Middle East, with air as the mode, but no origin-destination port pair.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor beyond the vendor in section 2 and state no operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say that air rates were far above last year in May and that the sources expected them to ease as capacity returned: «Despite the sharp increase in rates, Xeneta believes pricing pressures on shippers may begin to ease in June as capacity returns and demand growth moderates.»\n- Say that the cause the sources give is the Gulf disruption and fuel cost, and that the effect differs by lane.\n- Ask the client whether its air contract extends capacity at a surcharge, for how long, and what it would accept if rates fall.\n- Do not present the expected June easing as having happened: the pages hold nothing after early June.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: COST ALERT: A pricing lead, on the next air quote run, shortens quote validity on the Middle East lanes and the Europe-Asia lane to the length of the carrier's own rate review and records beside each quote the rate source and its date, so a re-quote after the expected easing can be compared with it.\n\n- A procurement lead asks each air carrier in writing what surcharge applies when an existing capacity contract is extended and for how many weeks, because the sources describe shippers accepting it.\n- A sea-air lead requests a sea-air quote for Asia to Europe cargo beside the air quote and records the transit time and rate of each, treating the vendor's own figures as claims to test.\n- An e-commerce lead lists clients whose flows rely on low-value parcels to the EU and tells them of the de minimis change in the article.\n\n## 8. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nParties and their stated interests. IATA: «IATA (International Air Transport Association) represents over 370 airlines accounting for some 85% of global air traffic.» Its Director General says «SAF production growth fell short of expectations as poorly designed mandates stalled momentum in the fledgling SAF industry.» Fuel suppliers in Europe, per IATA: «In Europe, ReFuelEU Aviation has sharply increased costs amid limited SAF capacity and oligopolistic supply chains. Fuel suppliers have widened their profit margins to such an extent that airlines pay up to five times more than the price of conventional jet fuel and double the market price of SAF.» For the UK, «The UK’s SAF mandate has triggered price spikes, leaving airlines to absorb the burden.» The cost to airlines is put at «airlines paid a premium of USD 2.9 billion for the limited 1.9 Mt of SAF available in 2025. Of this, USD 1.4 billion reflects the standard SAF price premium over conventional fuel.» IATA also says «The recent European Commission STIP announcement is a step forward though it lacks a clear timeline.» IATA backs the international route: «supports the implementation of global mechanisms such as CORSIA to accelerate SAF deployment.» ICAO states the certification rule for the fuels that count under CORSIA: «CORSIA eligible fuels shall come from fuel producers that are certified by a Sustainability Certification Scheme (SCS) approved by the ICAO Council to perform this certification» *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a given SAF batch and producer meet the CORSIA certification rule quoted above, which the ICAO page states but does not apply to any fuel here.\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on IATA's description of mandates as poorly designed and of supplier margins as widened, IATA's interest is lighter mandates and production incentives, and its figures are an advocate's, so a forwarder should read the premium numbers as IATA's estimates and not as audited prices.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the e-SAF mandates and the airline targets, as IATA states them. «With e-SAF mandates approaching in the UK (2028) and EU (2030), it’s essential not to repeat the policy missteps seen with SAF.» «Without strong production incentives (as opposed to mandates), supply will fall short of targets.» IATA also says «compliance costs could escalate to EUR 29 billion by 2032 if targets aren’t met, as seems very likely with the current policy framework.» On the airline side, IATA says «many airlines that have committed to use 10% SAF by 2030 will be forced to reevaluate these commitments.» The long goal behind all of it: «The aviation sector has committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050», and SAF «it could contribute up to 65% of the reduction in emissions needed by aviation to reach net zero CO2 emissions by 2050.»\n\n- 9 December 2025: IATA publishes its SAF production estimates (2025 output 1.9 Mt, 2026 projection 2.4 Mt).\n- 2028: UK e-SAF mandate approaching.\n- 2030: EU e-SAF mandate approaching; airlines' 10% SAF by 2030 commitments to be reevaluated, per IATA.\n- 2032: compliance costs could escalate to EUR 29 billion if targets are not met, per IATA.\n- 2050: aviation sector net zero carbon emissions commitment.\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the 2028 and 2030 e-SAF dates and on IATA's cost-base figure, the next cost step for airlines is the e-SAF mandate years, and IATA expects supply to fall short if mandates and not incentives carry the load. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the exact obligation, obliged party and start date of the UK and EU e-SAF mandates, which this press release does not set out.\n\n## 4. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nCOST ALERT: sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the lower-carbon jet fuel that UK and EU rules push airlines to buy, costs a multiple of fossil jet fuel, and production is still a small share of airline fuel. Signal event: «Today, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) generally costs between 2 and 5 times more than fossil jet fuel.» The analysis, by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), is dated «October 6, 2025», and it adds: «The European Union Aviation Safety Agency estimated that the average production cost of SAF in 2024 ranged from €1,461 per tonne (for biofuels) to €7,695 per tonne (for e-fuels). We calculate that this is a cost premium of 2.1–10.6x compared with fossil jet fuel». On volume, the industry association ATAG reports: «Approximately 2.4 billion litres (1.92 million tonnes) of SAF was produced in 2025» and «SAF usage in 2025 represented 0.6% of the total fuel consumption by airlines, compared to 0.3% in 2024.» It adds that «Global SAF production has roughly doubled each year since 2018». Both sources are analyses by a research body and an industry association, not regulators. The pages hold no air cargo rate and no surcharge, so this brief serves the price, regulatory-link, client and action lenses and states no cargo charge.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nGovernments: «regions such as the United Kingdom and European Union have put SAF mandates in place with penalties for non-compliance», and «The United Kingdom has offered more than £200 million in upfront grant funding to second-generation SAF projects via its Advanced Fuels Fund». Airlines: «airlines have criticized the high cost of SAF purchases and called on regulators in these regions to review the timeline and trajectory of mandates amidst rising prices.» The industry association ATAG, a «not-for-profit association based in Switzerland», records that «In October 2021, the air transport industry committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050», and the standard that fuel meets before it flies is that «Commercial flights are currently permitted to fly with a blend of up to 50% SAF and conventional fossil-based kerosene». ICCT's own interest is to lower the cost: it argues for public and private investment, market measures and cost sharing. *Analytical inference:* resting on ICCT's statement that the cost of SAF is primarily driven by the cost of its feedstock, the price a buyer sees follows feedstock cost, and the mandates and the airlines' request to review their timelines are separate matters that neither source links to price.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the airline call to change mandate timing, and the start of UK support. «airlines have criticized the high cost of SAF purchases and called on regulators in these regions to review the timeline and trajectory of mandates amidst rising prices.» «This is paired with its SAF mandate and revenue certainty mechanism, which will take effect by the end of 2026». On supply, «SAF production capacity is expected to reach 22.5 billion litres (18 million tonnes) by 2030.» On price, «While e-fuel costs should come down when they arrive on the market around 2030, they are expected to remain far above the current price of fossil jet fuel.» Governments also «set a goal for aviation fuel in 2030 to be 5% less carbon intensive, by transitioning to SAF and lower carbon aviation fuels.» The long-run share: «It estimated that SAF will contribute between 38% and 58% of the emissions reductions needed to get to net zero by 2050.»\n\n- October 6, 2025: ICCT analysis puts SAF at 2 to 5 times fossil jet fuel.\n- by the end of 2026: UK SAF mandate and revenue certainty mechanism take effect, per ICCT; the page does not say whether they have.\n- 2030: ATAG expects production capacity of 22.5 billion litres; the ICAO governments goal of 5% less carbon intensive fuel; e-fuel costs expected to come down but stay far above fossil jet fuel.\n- 2050: air transport net zero carbon emissions commitment.\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the two 2030 statements, 2030 is the year when both supply capacity and the e-fuel price are expected to move, so contract terms that fix a SAF cost today would be tested around then. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the penalties, scope and start dates of the UK and EU SAF mandates, which these pages mention but do not set out.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nCause and chain as the sources state it. Cost driver, as ICCT says: «The cost of SAF is primarily driven by the cost of its feedstock.» Supply risk: «It takes up to 5 years for SAF projects to reach final investment decision», and «fewer than 30% of SAF projects globally have reached final investment decision» UK cost flow: «The revenue certainty mechanism allows SAF producers to enter into a 15-year contract with a counterparty to set a fixed guaranteed strike price (GSP) on fuel production.» «The UK revenue certainty mechanism is funded by a levy on aviation fuel suppliers that covers the cost of SAF payments and administrative overhead for the counterparty.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the 2 to 5 times price multiple and on the UK levy sitting on aviation fuel suppliers, an air carrier buying SAF or paying a fuel supplier that carries the levy has a higher fuel cost than on fossil jet fuel, and a forwarder buying air capacity may see that cost arrive in carrier fuel or environmental surcharges. The sources state no pass-through from fuel supplier to airline or from airline to freight invoice, so the effect by lane and cargo vertical requires each carrier's own charge terms. A cost route the source does state for customers: they can «partner with businesses to procure voluntary SAF via Scope 3 certificates», and «they can be an effective way for customers to mitigate the costs of SAF procurement at any location around the world.» Corridor identity: the sources are global, name no origin-destination port pair and no airport pair, so the signal is tied to no single lane.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026: the sources name no competing forwarder and no competing operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say that SAF is a drop-in fuel whose obstacle is economic: «the barriers to increased SAF deployment are economic and political, rather than technical.»\n- Say that SAF is small and costly today: it is «SAF usage in 2025 represented 0.6% of the total fuel consumption by airlines, compared to 0.3% in 2024.»\n- Ask the client whether it wants to claim SAF emissions reductions through Scope 3 certificates, since ICCT says «they can be an effective way for customers to mitigate the costs of SAF procurement at any location around the world.»\n- Do not quote one SAF price multiple as settled: ICCT gives 2 to 5 times and also a 2.1 to 10.6 times range by fuel pathway.\n\n*Operational implication:* resting on the ICCT figures that depend on the fuel pathway, a client quote on air freight with a SAF element needs the pathway named before a multiple is used.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: COST ALERT: A sustainability-product lead, at the next quarterly review of airline partner offers, asks each air carrier whether it sells SAF emissions reductions to customers through Scope 3 certificates and on what registry terms, and records the answers in the client proposal template.\n\n- A pricing lead asks, at the next air fuel surcharge review, whether any UK or EU SAF mandate cost sits in the carrier's surcharge line and from which date, and records the answer beside the lane's quote.\n- A contracts lead adds, at the next air carrier agreement renewal, a request for written notice before a SAF-related line is added to a surcharge.\n\n## 8.    "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nCOST ALERT: a war in the Middle East has choked the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea passage out of the Persian Gulf, and fuel and transport costs are higher than before the conflict. Signal event, as the International Energy Agency (IEA) states it: «The war in the region that began on 28 February has impeded energy trade flows through the Strait, creating the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market». It adds that «Traffic through the Strait has been essentially halted by the conflict» and that «Around 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade transited the Strait in 2025, and options for oil flows to bypass the Strait of Hormuz are limited.» The price moves the IEA gives: «Brent futures, the global benchmark for crude prices, were roughly one-third above their pre-conflict levels in late May.» «Aviation activity is also running well below normal levels, helping to ease some of the pressure on jet fuel prices, which nearly tripled after Middle Eastern exports were cut off.» «Dutch TTF, the European benchmark for natural gas prices, rose by more than 40% between late February and late May.» These price figures are the IEA's late May readings; the pages hold no later price. The baseline volume tables are from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), whose page states «Last Updated: March 3, 2026», and they run to the first half of 2025, so they describe flows before the war. The pages hold no freight rate and no carrier charge, so this brief serves the price, operational, client and action lenses and states no rate.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nParties and their stated positions. The IEA, an energy agency of member countries: «On 11 March, IEA Member countries unanimously agreed to take emergency collective action to respond to the major disruptions in oil markets, making 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks available». Producers outside the Gulf: only «Only Saudi Arabia and the UAE have operational crude pipelines that could potentially reroute flows to bypass the Strait, with an estimated 3.5 mb/d to 5.5 mb/d of available capacity.» The Gulf as a supplier: «The Gulf region is a key source of exports of refined oil products to global markets, notably for middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel.» «Nearly 3 mb/d of refining capacity in the region has shut due to attacks and a lack of viable export outlets.» The UN Trade and Development body UNCTAD describes the Strait as «carrying around a quarter of global seaborne oil trade and significant volumes of liquefied natural gas and fertilizers», and says «Continued monitoring is essential to assess evolving risks and their potential impacts.» The pages name the governments and producers as parties but name no carrier, forwarder or shipper as a party. *Analytical inference:* resting on the stated absence of bypass routes beyond the Saudi and UAE pipelines, producers cannot offset the closure, so the price pressure persists until flows resume rather than being traded away.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: «resuming flows through the Strait of Hormuz remains the single most important variable in easing the pressure on energy supplies, prices and the global economy.» Further consequences the IEA states: «The Ras Laffan facility in Qatar, which is the largest liquefaction facility in the world, has been offline since it was first attacked on 2 March.» «delaying the anticipated global LNG supply wave by at least two years»; «Short-term supply losses and slower capacity growth could result in a cumulative loss of around 120 bcm of LNG supply between 2026 and 2030.» The EIA adds a supply-side step: «By 2027, the UAE plans to build another 1.5 million b/d pipeline circumventing the strait».\n\n- March 3, 2026: EIA chokepoints analysis last updated, a baseline to the first half of 2025.\n- 2026 to 2030: around 120 bcm of cumulative LNG supply loss, per the IEA.\n- 2027: the UAE plans a further 1.5 million b/d bypass pipeline, per the EIA.\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the IEA statement that resuming flows is the single most important variable, the observable that would turn this from a cost watch into a settled cost level is Strait of Hormuz traffic, and the pages give no date for it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which carrier surcharge clauses and insurance terms let a carrier pass the higher costs to a shipper, which the pages do not address.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nCause: traffic through the Strait is essentially halted. Mechanical consequence the sources state: «The blockage of oil transit through a major chokepoint, even temporarily, can lead to substantial supply delays and higher shipping costs, resulting in higher world energy prices.» The EIA gives the pre-war baseline, not the volume now stuck: «In 1H25, total oil flows through the strait averaged 20.9 million b/d, or the equivalent of about 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption, and one-quarter of total global maritime traded oil.» Effect on transport cost as UNCTAD states it: «Higher energy, fertilizer and transport costs – including freight rates, bunker fuel prices and insurance premiums – may increase food costs». On crude, UNCTAD says «Oil markets have reacted quickly, with Brent crude prices now rising above $90 per barrel»; the UNCTAD page is undated, so read it beside the IEA late May reading. Route effects already seen at the neighbouring passages: «after Yemen-based Houthi militia attacks on commercial ships transiting the Red Sea started in November 2023, some vessels began taking longer, more costly routes around the Cape of Good Hope» and «About 4.9 million b/d of crude oil and petroleum products transited the Suez Canal and the SUMED pipeline in 1H25, and an estimated 4.2 million b/d also transited the Bab el-Mandeb.» The Suez Canal and SUMED pipeline are the Egyptian link in that route.    "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: California has started the official check of how much renewable electricity its electricity suppliers bought in the four years 2021 to 2024, and the adopted result is what the later compliance determination rests on. Signal event, from the California Energy Commission (CEC), the state energy agency: «RPS Compliance Period 4 Summary Claims Reports, Notice of Availability, and 25 Staff Draft Verification Results Reports» are now available. The CEC states that «Compliance Period 4 covers the reporting years 2021-2024.» and that «The program sets continuously escalating renewable energy procurement requirements for the state’s load-serving entities.» «The California Energy Commission verifies RPS claims.» It also states: «The verification results are not a compliance determination.» The pages are state agency publications of the program, not an analysis. They hold no freight, transport rate or port content, so this brief serves the regulatory-link, client and action lenses and states no cost to a freight operator.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nParties and their roles as the CEC and the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) state them. The suppliers: «Load-serving entities (LSEs) include POUs, investor-owned utilities (IOUs), electricity service providers (ESPs), and community choice aggregators (CCAs).» The CPUC: «The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) implements and administers RPS compliance rules for California’s retail sellers of electricity, which include investor-owned utilities (IOUs), electric service providers (ESPs) and community choice aggregators (CCAs).» The CEC may enforce on the publicly owned utilities: «The Energy Commission is authorized to issue violation notices for noncompliance and refer the POU to the California Air Resources Board to assess penalties.» Reporting rhythm: «Retail Sellers and POUs must report their RPS procurement claims annually to the Energy Commission on or before July 1», and «Retail sellers are required to submit Annual RPS Compliance Reports on August 1 each year to demonstrate progress towards the RPS procurement requirements.» The pages name no freight company, carrier or forwarder as a party. *Analytical inference:* resting on the statement that load-serving entities carry the procurement requirement, the party with the compliance exposure is the electricity supplier, and an electricity customer such as a warehouse or a charging site is not named as obligated.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: «The Energy Commission adopts verification results reports for each compliance period. Once the results are adopted, the process begins to determine if POUs comply with statutes and the RPS POU regulations.» Before that, «Prior to consideration at a business meeting, CEC staff will prepare a draft verification results report for review and comment. If adopted, a final verification results report will be prepared.» The path of the requirement, as the CEC states it: «33 percent by the end of 2020 44 percent by the end of 2024 52 percent by the end of 2027 60 percent by the end of 2030», in periods «Compliance Period 4: 2021-2024 Compliance Period 5: 2025-2027 Compliance Period 6: 2028-2030» A supporting step: «WREGIS announced its agreement with its current software provider ends on December 31, 2027, and will not be extended.»\n\n- 2021-2024: Compliance Period 4, now at the draft verification stage.\n- December 31, 2027: the software agreement of WREGIS ends and will not be extended.\n- 2027: renewable procurement target of 52 percent by the end of the year.\n- 2030: renewable procurement target of 60 percent by the end of the year.\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the staged path of draft, adoption and then compliance determination, the draft reports are not yet a finding against any supplier, and the point where a supplier's compliance becomes known is the adoption of its results. *Analytical inference:* resting on the periods and targets above, a supplier's verified share for Compliance Period 5 (2025-2027) and 6 (2028-2030) will be measured against 52 and 60 percent, so the share an operator is told today is a past-period figure; and resting on the WREGIS statement, the tracking system its claims rely on needs new software after December 31, 2027, a change the page says nothing more about. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which load-serving entity supplies a given California site and whether its Compliance Period 4 results have been adopted, which these pages do not state for any named supplier.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nCause: the verification of procurement claims. Mechanism as the CEC states it: «RPS targets are verified based on a multiyear accounting period rather than annual accounting.» «Compliance with the RPS program is measured in eligible renewable energy credits (RECs) and evaluated on a multi-year compliance period basis.» The check on quality: the CEC «ensures each REC claimed by retail sellers' is eligible for compliance and not double-counted». The tracking system behind it: WREGIS «is an independent renewable energy certificate tracking system. California’s Renewables Portfolio Standard program relies on WREGIS to support program administration».\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the statement that the RPS requirement sits on load-serving entities and is verified by renewable energy credits, a freight operator buying electricity in California for a warehouse or a charging site buys from a supplier whose renewable share is set by this process, so the supplier's verified percentage is the figure to ask for when the operator reports emissions from purchased electricity. The pages state no electricity price effect, no cost pass-through to customers and no emissions factor, so any cost or emissions effect by site or cargo vertical requires the operator's own supplier data. Corridor identity: the sources are about California electricity procurement, name no origin-destination port pair and no transport mode, so the signal is tied to no single lane.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026: the sources name no competing forwarder and no competing operator position.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say that the draft reports are not a finding: «The verification results are not a compliance determination.»\n- Ask the client which California electricity supplier serves its sites, since the requirement sits on suppliers and a customer is not named as obligated.\n- Do not tell a client that a California supplier has met or missed its target on the strength of these pages: the draft stage is not an adoption.\n\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: MONITORING: A sustainability data lead, at the next annual emissions inventory update, records for each California site which load-serving entity supplies its electricity and asks that supplier for its verified RPS percentage once the CEC adopts the Compliance Period 4 results.\n\n- A procurement lead asks, before the next California warehouse or charging contract renewal, which entity supplies the site and whether the contract names the supplier's RPS verification status.\n- A reporting lead adds, at the next emissions report close, a field for the supplier type (investor-owned utility, community choice aggregator or electricity service provider) beside each California site.\n\n## 8.
