   "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: this item follows the Getting to Zero Coalition and its work on green shipping corridors, routes on which ships running on zero-emission fuels are being set up. Signal event: the Coalition's news list for the latest period shows «4 June 2026 New consortium to advance e-fuel green corridor between Brazil and Belgium» and «7 May 2026 Getting to Zero Coalition report highlights members’ progress and systemic bottlenecks» Earlier entries show the direction: «1 December 2023 Green corridors expand in number and maturation, new report finds» and then «19 November 2024 Green corridors grow by 40% worldwide, but face a \"feasibility wall\", says Global Maritime Forum report» and «27 November 2025 China, India, and Brazil move on green shipping corridors as industry awaits climate regulations»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the headlines show corridors increasing in number through 2023 and 2024, then meeting a stated obstacle, a \"feasibility wall\", and by late 2025 moving in China, India and Brazil while the industry waits for climate regulation; the pages give the headlines only, with no corridor count, fuel volume or price beyond the figure in the 2024 headline. The pages hold no competitor or price content, so this brief serves the route, regulatory, client and technology lenses only.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: «The Getting to Zero Coalition is a powerful alliance of more than 200 organisations (including over 180 private companies) within the maritime, energy, infrastructure, and finance sectors.» «The Coalition is managed by the Global Maritime Forum, which initially founded it together with the World Economic Forum and Friends of Ocean Action.» The Coalition states its work: «The Coalition’s strategy focuses on two key objectives: fostering progress around first-mover projects and preparing a full, just, and equitable transition at scale.» «Working groups include green corridor task forces, a book and claim task force, a policy action group, and a Latin America task force.» Its reach among governments: «It is also endorsed by the governments of 14 countries.» It claims policy influence: «Advocacy through the Coalition has also played a key role in recent policy developments, including the International Maritime Organization’s decision to introduce much more ambitious targets, the European Union’s Fit for 55, and national frameworks for international shipping.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the group is an industry alliance that wants zero-emission fuels and ships available at scale and affordable, and it uses corridors as first movers; the pages name no freight forwarder as a driver and state no price or commitment that a customer would receive.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the rule that would make corridor fuels a requirement rather than a choice sits at the International Maritime Organization, and the news list shows it undecided: «17 October 2025 Negotiations at International Maritime Organization adjourn without a decision on shipping’s Net-Zero Framework» and later «6 May 2026 Negotiations signal progress but uncertainty remains on the Net-Zero Framework» The Coalition's own target: «The Coalition is committed to getting commercially viable zero-emission vessels powered by zero-emission fuels into operation by 2030.» «Hitting this milestone is essential if we are to achieve maritime shipping’s moon-shot ambition of full decarbonisation by 2050.» On the pace, its list shows «25 September 2024 Shipping off track to meet 5% zero-emission fuel target by 2030 as new report issues ‘serious wakeup call’»\n\n- 2026: «31 August 2023 First-of-a-kind ammonia-powered gas carriers could be commercially viable from 2026, new study finds»\n- 2029: «30 October 2025 Study shows South Africa-Europe shipping route could run on green ammonia by 2029»\n- 2030: «The Coalition is committed to getting commercially viable zero-emission vessels powered by zero-emission fuels into operation by 2030.»\n- 2050: «Hitting this milestone is essential if we are to achieve maritime shipping’s moon-shot ambition of full decarbonisation by 2050.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a corridor stays a voluntary project while the international rule is undecided, and the 2030 milestone and the 2050 ambition are the Coalition's goals and not legal deadlines; the sources do not say when or whether the Net-Zero Framework will be adopted.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe pages state no price, surcharge or contract term for a corridor service, so the cost to a forwarder is not held. What they hold on routes: «20 September 2024 Action needed to meet growing demand for sustainable fuels on Rotterdam-Singapore shipping corridor» *Analytical inference:* this headline names a port pair and a mode together, which makes it the one lane fixed in the headlines; the pages do not say that any carrier offers or prices a zero-emission service on it. On how buyers might reach the fuel, the news list records «22 August 2024 Aggregating demand can help the shipping industry crack the code on scaling sustainable fuels» and «3 July 2023 Major maritime companies agree to develop book and claim approaches in order to accelerate shipping’s decarbonisation transition» *Analytical inference:* the pages hold only a task-force name and a headline on book and claim, so they do not say how such an approach would work, what it would cost or what share a forwarder would bear.\n\nCorridor identity: the headline above names Rotterdam and Singapore with shipping; other headlines name Brazil and Belgium, South Africa and Europe, and no port pairs, so the lane in each of those is not fixed.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor position that bears on a forwarder's market standing.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Say who runs it: «The Getting to Zero Coalition is a powerful alliance of more than 200 organisations (including over 180 private companies) within the maritime, energy, infrastructure, and finance sectors.»\n- Say that corridor growth has limits: «19 November 2024 Green corridors grow by 40% worldwide, but face a \"feasibility wall\", says Global Maritime Forum report»\n- Ask the client whether any of its cargo moves on a lane that has a green corridor project and whether it wants that option priced.\n- Do not tell a client that a corridor service is available or priced: no page states either.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: MONITORING: An ocean procurement lead, before the next ocean tender, asks each ocean carrier on the workspace's main trade lanes in writing whether it takes part in a green corridor or a book and claim scheme, which corridor and which fuel, and records the answers beside each lane's quote.\n\n- A sustainability lead lists which of the workspace's lanes match a corridor named by the Coalition, so a carrier's answer can be placed.\n- A policy lead records each news entry on the Net-Zero Framework with its date, since that decision is the stated trigger.\n\n## 8. Sources\n\n- Global Maritime Forum, Getting to Zero Coalition page (coalition manager and industry association): https://globalmaritimeforum.org/getting-to-zero-coalition\n",

What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: the World Bank is moving money toward lower-carbon transport through a small grant facility that draws in much larger World Bank financing, but its evaluators said in a November 21, 2022 note that the lending was timid. Signal event, from the World Bank's Global Facility to Decarbonize Transport (GFDT) pages: «The 2025 GFDT Annual Report covers January 1, 2025, to December 31, 2025.» «GFDT-funded activities delivered advisory services to 58 government entities, provided technical assistance or capacity building in over 30 countries, and supported the preparation of 20 flagship studies, tools, and strategies.» The result: «This upstream work catalyzed six World Bank-financed transport investments under implementation, with three additional operations under preparation—representing $3.6 billion in current and anticipated financing.» Against the facility's size: «for every $1 disbursed, $105 has been mobilized in World Bank financing for transport decarbonization, rising to $328 as projects advance and additional financing is unlocked.» The earlier year for comparison: «Throughout 2024, GFDT-funded activities delivered advisory services to 55 government entities, provided technical support to 28 countries». What the facility is: «The Global Facility to Decarbonize Transport (GFDT) is a multi-donor trust fund that accelerates innovation and investment in low-carbon mobility solutions.» The pages describe passenger and public transport examples; they name no freight or port project. The pages hold no price or rate content, so this brief serves the competitive, regulatory-link, client and action lenses and states no cost to a freight operator.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nParties and their stated interests. The World Bank and the World Resources Institute co-host the Transforming Transportation conference, and «Our lead sponsor is FedEx.» The Bank's scale: «approximately $40 billion of transport portfolio investments throughout the world». Its stated problem: «the financing need for sustainable transport is beyond what government and MDBs altogether can provide. We must mobilize capital at a greater scale» Its direction of travel: «The World Bank has steadily increased the number of projects with decarbonization content, especially in low income countries». The Independent Evaluation Group is the Bank's evaluator: «The Independent Evaluation Group (IEG) evaluates the development effectiveness of the World Bank Group.» *Analytical inference:* resting on the stated gap between transport financing need and what governments and development banks can supply, the Bank's interest is to use a small grant facility to draw in private and public capital, and FedEx is named as the lead sponsor of the conference, although the pages state no FedEx position or commitment.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the move of projects from preparation to financing. «This upstream work catalyzed six World Bank-financed transport investments under implementation, with three additional operations under preparation—representing $3.6 billion in current and anticipated financing.» The 2024 report adds the climate effect expected: «GFDT-funded activities are projected to avoid ~508,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent (tCO₂e) from the two approved investments, rising to ~3 million tCO₂e when including the additional eight in preparation.» The longer frame: transport «the sector emits approximately 24 percent of the global total of energy-related carbon emissions and, without aggressive measures, the World Bank expects emissions from transport to grow 60 percent by 2050.»\n\n- November 21, 2022: IEG insight note on transport decarbonization published; it finds lending timid.\n- March 20, 2024: Transforming Transportation 2024 held on mobilizing finance for climate action.\n- December 31, 2025: end of the period covered by the 2025 GFDT Annual Report.\n- 2050: the World Bank expects transport emissions to grow 60 percent without aggressive measures.\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the six investments under implementation and three under preparation, the near-term observable is whether the three operations under preparation reach financing; the pages give no dates for them. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any financed project carries procurement or eligibility rules that apply to a foreign freight provider, which the pages do not address.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nCause: development financing for transport decarbonization. Scale and base: «the sector emits approximately 24 percent of the global total of energy-related carbon emissions and, without aggressive measures, the World Bank expects emissions from transport to grow 60 percent by 2050.» Another measure on a different basis: «Transport accounts for 20% of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions and, with urbanization and motorization on the rise in developing countries, this could grow to 60% by 2050.» The Bank's own assessment: «This first EIN identifies patterns in the World Bank’s transport decarbonization work and finds opportunities for bolder actions.» Specifically, «Nevertheless, transport decarbonization in World Bank lending remains timid against the needed contributions to the Climate Change Action Plan»; «Country-specific decarbonization diagnostics and analytical work has been limited»; «The World Bank has rarely measured transport decarbonization directly.» Examples the pages give are public transport: «BRT is enjoying growing popularity in Africa, where six systems are already operational and another ten are under development.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* resting on the Bank's examples being bus and rail passenger systems and on its evaluators' finding that decarbonization is rarely measured directly, financed projects in the pages are more likely to change urban passenger transport in low and middle income countries than freight lanes, and any freight effect on a lane requires the project documents of the country concerned. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nMONITORING: this item follows the 2026 International Roadcheck, a North American roadside inspection campaign run by the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) for commercial trucks. Signal event: «From May 12 to 14, enforcement personnel throughout North America will inspect commercial motor vehicles and commercial motor vehicle drivers for compliance with vehicle, cargo and driver regulatory requirements as part of the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance’s (CVSA) 72-hour inspection, enforcement and data-collection initiative, International Roadcheck.» The driver focus is set out as «The driver focus for this year’s International Roadcheck is on electronic logging device (ELD) tampering, falsification or manipulation.» and the vehicle focus as «This year’s International Roadcheck vehicle focus is cargo securement.»\n\nTrade press reports the first day of data. FreightWaves, citing federal inspection records, states: «Day 1 produced 1,580 inspections across 1,417 distinct carriers. Total violations logged: 2,637. Out-of-service orders issued: 496.» It puts that at «a 31.4% out-of-service rate against total inspection volume» and sets it against the full 2025 event: «Across all 56,178 inspections conducted during the complete 2025 Roadcheck, CVSA reported an 18.1% vehicle OOS rate.» The same article embeds a post from FreightWaves that gives a different 2025 figure: «Last year (2025) saw an 18.4% OOS rate for vehicles.» *Analytical inference:* the two 2025 vehicle figures in one article differ by 0.3 points, so the 2025 comparison point is not settled by this source; both are shown and the day-one rate sits well above either. The day-one rate is also a one-day sample from trade-press analysis of inspection records, not a CVSA result. The pages hold no competitor, technology or research content, so this brief serves the cost, client, route and regulatory lenses.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: «CVSA is a nonprofit organization composed of local, state, provincial, territorial and federal commercial motor vehicle safety officials and industry representatives in Canada, Mexico and the U.S.» Its stated aim: «The Alliance aims to prevent commercial motor vehicle crashes, injuries and fatalities and believes that collaboration between government and industry improves road safety and saves lives.» The Alliance states why it picked this year's focus areas from last year's violation counts: «Last year, falsification of record of duty status was the second most-cited violation out of all driver violations, at 58,382 violations.» and «And five out of the top 10 driver violations were related to hours of service or ELDs.» For cargo, it cites «In 2025, 18,108 violations were issued because cargo was not secured to prevent leaking/spilling/blowing/falling and 16,054 violations were issued for vehicle components or dunnage not being secured.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the party that sets the focus is a body of enforcement officials and industry members, and it chose the focus from its own prior-year violation counts above, so the emphasis is a signal of where inspector attention goes this year rather than a new rule. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nCOST ALERT: this item follows the price of natural gas in three regions: the European benchmark (Dutch TTF), the East Asian benchmark (Japan-Korea Marker, JKM) and the U.S. benchmark (Henry Hub). Signal event: the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) wrote on «April 28, 2026 International LNG prices rise amid Strait of Hormuz closure» that «Prices for natural gas in Europe and Asia have diverged from those in the United States since the February 28 closure of the Strait of Hormuz.» On the numbers it gives: «Futures prices for liquified natural gas (LNG) delivery to the Title Transfer Facility (TTF), the European benchmark price, increased to $14.80 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) for the week ending April 24, 35% higher than before the closure, according to data from Bloomberg L.P.» «In East Asia, the front-month futures price for the benchmark Japan-Korea Marker (JKM), rose 51% over the same period to $16.02/MMBtu.» The U.S. went the other way: «In contrast, natural gas prices at the U.S. benchmark Henry Hub have decreased 9% since February 28 due to limited opportunities for increasing LNG exports in the near term and ample domestic seasonal natural gas storage and supply»\n\nFor scale on the U.S. side, the EIA's year review says «In 2025, the wholesale U.S. natural gas spot price at the national benchmark Henry Hub in Louisiana averaged $3.52 per million British thermal units (MMBtu)» A delayed exchange page for Henry Hub futures, a separate source, shows: «Globex Code NGN26 Last 3.220 Change -0.116 (-3.48%) Volume 146,564 Trading Simulator Watchlists Last Updated 05 Jun 2026 02:16:22 PM CT» *Analytical inference:* the EIA article's TTF and JKM prices and the Henry Hub price on the exchange page are for different dates and contracts, so no like-for-like spread between Europe, Asia and the U.S. is held; what is held is the direction of each move since February 28 (up 35% and up 51% in Europe and East Asia, down 9% in the U.S.). The pages hold no competitor, technology or research content, so this brief serves the price, cost, client and route lenses only.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: «QatarEnergy declared force majeure on March 4, which has forced Asian buyers who import over 80% of Qatari gas to compete for spot cargoes on global markets to replace lost contract volumes.» The scale of the loss is stated: «The closure of the strait has affected over 10 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of global LNG supplies.» On the U.S. side, the EIA says that «Operators already run U.S. LNG terminals at high utilization rates, limiting additional natural gas export growth» and «The export terminal capacity utilization in March amounted to 94% of the maximum DOE-approved export levels.» The article names buyers in Asia competing for spot cargoes and exporters in Qatar and the United States, and gives no stated aim for any of them beyond the replacement of lost volumes.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the strait closure removed supply from the global market, Asian buyers then bid for the remaining spot cargoes, and U.S. terminals were already close to full use, so the U.S. could not send enough gas abroad to close the price gap; this follows the force majeure, supply loss and utilization sentences above and is the EIA's own reasoning for why the three prices diverged.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the EIA states that European storage was low at the end of winter and that refilling it adds to spot demand: «European natural gas storage inventories finished the winter season at 28% full, below the five-year average of 41%» «which will likely require more spot cargoes to refill storage inventories prior to next winter.» The EIA adds that «Although average weekly TTF prices have fallen from a three-year high reached in mid-March, prices remain elevated compared with February.» and that «JKM prices are likely to move with weather-related spot demand.» On supply it expects that «We expect U.S. LNG exports will increase, but only by a small portion of the missing volumes.» and that «we expect that approximately 2.4 Bcf/d of DOE-authorized export capacity will come online between April and December 2026.»\n\n- April 28, 2026: the EIA article on the divergence, «April 28, 2026 International LNG prices rise amid Strait of Hormuz closure»\n- December 2026: end of the window in which «we expect that approximately 2.4 Bcf/d of DOE-authorized export capacity will come online between April and December 2026»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the EIA's own expectation is that U.S. export growth covers only a small part of the missing volume, and that European storage refilling will likely require more spot cargoes before next winter; the article states these expectations and gives no price forecast.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nThe pages state no freight rate, surcharge or fuel cost and tie the gas prices to supply and storage only. The one transport fact stated is that «No laden LNG vessels are known to have crossed the strait between March 1 and April 24, according to Kpler data.» *Analytical inference:* gas priced at these levels reaches a forwarder's costs only through the contracts of its counterparties that are indexed to a gas or energy price, and the pages do not say which counterparties those are, how fast a move reaches an invoice, or which cargo verticals are affected; the size and timing therefore depend on each counterparty's own terms. The exchange page describes its contract as «Manage risk using highly liquid Henry Hub Natural Gas futures and options.» so a futures price is available for the U.S. benchmark for those who hedge. Corridor identity: the article names the Strait of Hormuz and Qatar's Ras Laffan export facility and no origin-destination port pair with a transport mode together, so the signal is tied to no single lane.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor position that bears on a forwarder's market standing.*\n\n## 6. What's Moving and What Triggered It\n\nCOST ALERT: this item follows the price of a carbon allowance, the permit a company holds to cover each tonne of greenhouse gas it emits, in the European Union Emissions Trading System and in other carbon markets. Signal event: a live carbon price page shows, with its own column headings, «Last Change YTD COMPLIANCE MARKETS European Union €78.23 +1.93% -15.35% UK $52.33 0.00% -29.71%» The page carries no time stamp for these prices in the text this site holds, so they are read as the page stood when it was collected. For comparison, the International Carbon Action Partnership (ICAP) factsheet gives the 2025 averages for the European system: «Average auction price (2025) EUR 73.43 (USD 82.97) Average secondary market price (2025) EUR 74.35 (USD 84.01)»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the live European Union price sits above the 2025 average secondary market price, while the page's year-to-date column shows it down on the year; the two sources differ in date and currency presentation, so no like-for-like change is stated here. On scale, the system's limit for 2026 is «Cap or total emissions limit 1,185.4 MtCO2e (2026, electricity and heat generation, industrial manufacturing and maritime transport), 26.2 MtCO2e (2026, aviation)» Separately, for carbon pricing worldwide and not the European system alone, the World Bank reports: «Carbon pricing revenues exceeded $100 billion in 2024, according to a new World Bank report released today.» and that «around 28% of global greenhouse gas emissions are now covered by a carbon price» The pages hold no competitor, technology or research content, so this brief serves the price, cost, client and regulatory lenses only.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the European Union institutions set the rules and the market runs on them. ICAP calls the system «It remains a cornerstone instrument of the EU’s policy framework to combat climate change and reduce GHG emissions cost-effectively.» The way allowances reach the market is stated: «Auctioning is the main method of distributing allowances, with free allocation, based on benchmarks, used to address the risk of carbon leakage.» Cost falls on the emitters: «Every year, covered entities must surrender allowances for their emissions under the EU ETS 1.» On linking with another system, ICAP reports that «In May 2025, the EU and the UK announced their intention to link their respective ETSs.» and that «the EU Council granted the Commission a negotiating mandate, authorising it to start formal talks with the UK on an ETS linking agreement.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the demand for allowances is set by law, and the supply by a falling cap, so the price on the live page is where those two meet; the pages state no position of any trading firm and no forecast of the price.\n\n## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers\n\nConversion trigger: the next dated step that brings the allowance price into new freight costs is the border carbon mechanism: «By September 30, 2027, EU importers will have to surrender CBAM certificates for 2.5% of the GHG emissions embedded in relevant goods imported in 2026.» The cap keeps tightening: «The factor is set at 2.2% per year (of 2008 to 2012 baseline emissions) for the period 2021 to 2023, 4.3% for 2024 to 2027 and 4.4% from 2028.» A second system starts later: «EU ETS 2, to start in 2028.» For aviation, «This ‘stop-the-clock’ limited scope of the EU ETS for aviation was extended until the end of 2026.» The long-run climate targets the system serves are: «By 2030 : Reduce net emissions to at least 55% below 1990 GHG levels»; «By 2040: Reduce net emissions to 90% below 1990 GHG levels»; «By 2050 : Net zero (European Climate Law)».\n\n- September 30, 2027: «By September 30, 2027, EU importers will have to surrender CBAM certificates for 2.5% of the GHG emissions embedded in relevant goods imported in 2026.»\n- 2028: «The factor is set at 2.2% per year (of 2008 to 2012 baseline emissions) for the period 2021 to 2023, 4.3% for 2024 to 2027 and 4.4% from 2028.»\n- 2028: «EU ETS 2, to start in 2028»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the dated steps above are the sources' schedule: the reduction factor rises from 4.3% to 4.4% in 2028, a second system starts in 2028, and the aviation limit runs to the end of 2026; the sources give no price forecast, and the live page's year-to-date column shows the price down on the year, so no direction of price is stated here.\n\n## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes\n\nCause: allowance cost reaches operators that must surrender allowances. For shipping: «In 2025, the compliance obligation for maritime transport operators commenced. Shipping companies must surrender allowances equal to 40% of their verified 2024 CO 2 emissions and 70% for 2025.» «From 2026 onwards, the scope of covered emissions in the sector expands to include CH 4 and N 2 O.» For aviation: «In aviation, free emission allowances for operators were down to 50% in 2025 and are fully phased out as of 2026.» On the import side: «From 2026, the definitive stage of the EU’s CBAM starts.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* where a shipping company or aircraft operator must surrender allowances for the emissions of a voyage or flight that touches the European system, its cost rises with the allowance price on the live page; the sources do not say whether, how fast or in what share that cost is passed on in a charge to a forwarder, so any pass-through depends on each carrier's terms and no cargo vertical is singled out by any page. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which shipping and aviation movements of the workspace fall inside the covered scope and the surrender percentages above, whether the importer duty to surrender border mechanism certificates for 2.5% of embedded emissions by September 30, 2027 reaches the workspace's imports; and which voyages fall under the wider gas scope (CH 4 and N 2 O) from 2026; all of which only the instruments' text can settle.\n\nLinked items: this price is one of two instruments the platform links under the global jurisdiction; a separate research brief on this site covers a planned pricing measure for shipping fuels, and its terms are in that brief, not on these pages. Corridor identity: the pages describe a trading system and name no origin-destination port pair with a transport mode together, so the signal is tied to no single lane.\n\n## 5. Competitive Implications\n\n*No content for this section as of 2026-11-01: the pages name no competitor position that bears on a forwarder's market standing.*\n\n## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points\n\n- Name the reference: ICAP reports the 2025 averages for the European system as «Average auction price (2025) EUR 73.43 (USD 82.97) Average secondary market price (2025) EUR 74.35 (USD 84.01)»\n- Say that a carrier's charge for allowance cost, if it has one, depends on the carrier's own terms; no source states a standard pass-through.\n- Ask the client whether its contracts already name a published allowance price for any carbon-related charge.\n- Do not present the live page price as a forecast: it is a reading, and the sources give no price outlook.\n\n## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now\n\nAction now: COST ALERT: A pricing lead, at the next monthly review of charges on European Union moves, records the European Union allowance price from the live price page with its date beside the 2025 average secondary market price of EUR 74.35, and asks each shipping company and aircraft operator in writing which published allowance price its allowance-cost charge follows and when it resets.\n\n- A contract lead adds, at the next carrier agreement renewal, a clause naming the published allowance price and the reset day for any charge that carries allowance cost.\n- A data lead keeps a dated series of the live price so the year-to-date movement can be checked against the page's own column.\n\n## 8. Sources\n\n- CarbonCredits.com, Live Carbon Prices Today (price page, vendor): https://carboncredits.com/carbon-prices-today/\n- International Carbon Action Partnership, EU Emissions Trading System factsheet (system status report): https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/eu-emissions-trading-system-eu-ets\n- World Bank, press release on global carbon pricing revenues (intergovernmental body): https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/06/10/global-carbon-pricing-mobilizes-over-100-billion-for-public-budgets\n- Linked research brief on this site covering a planned pricing measure for shipping fuels\n",

The latest edition this site holds is the one with «Release Date: May 12, 2026». Signal event: «The Brent crude oil spot price increased sharply in April , reaching a high of $138 per barrel (b) on April 7 and averaging $117/b for the month, as the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz tightened global oil supplies.» The same edition sets the price against the years either side: «2024 2025 2026 projected 2027 projected Brent crude oil (dollars per barrel) 81 69 95 79» *Analytical inference:* the Brent crude oil price (the global oil benchmark) is shown at 69 dollars a barrel for 2025, 95 for 2026 as projected, and 79 for 2027 as projected, so the 2026 projection is the peak of the three years shown and the April average of 117 dollars sits well above the 2026 average projected.\n\nThe EIA's view of what comes next: «We expect global oil inventories will fall by an average of 8.5 million b/d in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), keeping Brent prices around $106/b in May and June.» On supply: «We assess that Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, and Bahrain collectively shut in 10.5 million barrels per day (b/d) of crude oil production in April.» And on stocks: «we forecast global oil inventories will decrease by 2.6 million b/d this year, compared with a 0.3 million b/d decrease in last month’s STEO.» The pages hold no competitor, technology or research content, so this brief serves the price, cost, client and route lenses only. This site holds the May 12, 2026 edition only; later editions are not held here, so the figures read as that edition's, not as current prices.\n\n## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want\n\nDriving parties: the EIA publishes the forecast and states its purpose: «The Annual Energy Outlook (AEO) presents an assessment by the U.S. Energy Information Administration of the outlook for energy markets through 2050.» The supply side is led by the producers named above and by OPEC: «The UAE announced its departure from OPEC, effective May 1, 2026.» On gas and related fuels the EIA says that «Global LNG prices remain elevated as a result of reduced flows through the Strait of Hormuz, with a wide spread between U.S. domestic natural gas prices and international markets.» and that propane flows to Asia as «leading to an increase in U.S propane exports in 2026 and 2027 as buyers in Asia replace lost supply from the Persian Gulf after the Strait of Hormuz closure.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the price move is driven by physical supply loss and slow reopening of the strait, not by a policy decision of the EIA, which only forecasts; the pages state no aim of any producer or buyer beyond replacing lost supply.\n\n## 3.
